'''''Aethusa cynapium''''' ('''fool's parsley''', '''fool's cicely''', or '''poison parsley''') is an [[annual plant|annual]] (rarely [[biennial plant|biennial]]) [[herb]] in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Apiaceae]], native to [[Europe]], western [[Asia]], and northwest [[Africa]]. It is the only member of the genus '''''Aethusa'''''. It is related to [[Conium maculatum|hemlock]] and [[Oenanthe (plant)|water-dropwort]], and like them it is [[poison]]ous,<ref>Clapham, Tutin, & Warburg: Flora of the British Isles, 2nd edition, page 524</ref> though less so than hemlock. It has been introduced into many other parts of the world and is a common weed in cultivated ground.<ref name="Britannica-1911">{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Fool's Parsley|volume=10|page=616}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Aethusa cynapium 002.JPG|left|thumb|Inflorescence of fool's parsley]]
''Aethusa cynapium'' has a [[:wikt:fusiform|fusiform]] root and a smooth hollow branched stem growing to about {{convert|80|cm|in|abbr=on}} high, with much divided (ternately pinnate) smooth [[Leaf|leaves]] with an unpleasant smell, and small compound [[umbel]]s of small irregular white [[flower]]s.<ref name="Britannica-1911"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Aethusa cynapium'' was given its accepted scientific name by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref name="POWO" /> It is the sole species in the genus ''Aethusa'' which is part of the family [[Apiaceae]].<ref>{{cite POWO |id=39623-1 |title=''Aethusa'' L. |access-date=4 September 2025}}</ref> 

It has three accepted [[subspecies]] according to [[Plants of the World Online]]:<ref name="POWO" />
* ''Aethusa cynapium'' subsp. ''cynapium''
* ''Aethusa cynapium'' subsp. ''elata'' {{Small|(Hoffm.) Schübl. & G.Martens}}
* ''Aethusa cynapium'' subsp. ''segetalis'' {{Small|(Boenn.) Schübl. & G.Martens}}

===Names===
The [[common name]]s for the species include ''fool's parsley'', ''dog poison'', ''dog's parsley'', ''garden hemlock'', and ''lesser hemlock''.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lawton |first1=Barbara Perry |date=2007 |title=Parsleys, Fennels, and Queen Anne's Lace : Herbs and Ornamentals From the Umbel Family |url=https://archive.org/details/parsleysfennelsq0000lawt |location=Portland, Oregon |publisher=Timber Press |pages=89-90 |isbn=978-0-88192-822-8 |oclc=68693534 |access-date=4 September 2025}}</ref>

== Chemical composition, toxicity and medical uses ==
''A. cynapium'' is poisonous when fresh, but safe if dried. ''A. cynapium'''s toxic effects are caused at least in part by [[cynopine]], which resembles [[coniine]] in its physical and chemical characters as well as physiological actions. The whole plant is toxic with this [[alkaloid]]. Toxins like cynopine are destroyed by drying. ''A. cynapium'' also contains [[trideca-7,9,11-trienoic acid]], [[aethusin]], [[aethusanol A]], [[aethusanol  B]], as well as [[flavone glycoside]]s such as [[rutoside]], [[narcissine]], and [[ascorbic acid]].<ref name="Dwivedi-2021">Dwivedi, H., Bhardwaj, M., & Kumar, G. (2021). A Comprehensive Study of Poisonous Plants of Family Apiaceae. In Apiaceae: Ecology, Uses and Toxicity (pp. 1–14). Nova Publisher, New York.</ref><ref name="WebMD">{{cite web|title=Fool's Parsley - Uses, Side Effects, and More|url=https://www.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-447/fools-parsley|website=WebMD|accessdate=2025-01-03}}</ref><ref name="Shri-2010">{{cite journal |last1=Shri |first1=Richa |last2=Bhutani |first2=K.K. |last3=Sharma |first3=Anupam |year=2010 |title=A new anxiolytic fatty acid from Aethusa cynapium |journal=Fitoterapia |volume=81 |issue=5 |pages=337–340 |doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2010.05.003|pmid=20472038 }}</ref>

The parts of ''A. cynapium'' that grow above the ground are sometimes used to make medicine. The plants has been used in traditional medicine to treat complaints in children, infantile cholera, summer diarrhea, convulsions, mental tension, sleep disorders, delirium, and as stomachic. ''A. cynapium'' has actually been shown to cause antianxiety effects in mice because it contains [[trideca-7,9,11-trienoic acid]].<ref name="Dwivedi-2021" /><ref name="WebMD" /><ref name="Shri-2010" />

Poisoning from ''A. cynapium'' results in symptoms of heat in the mouth and throat. A post-mortem examination has shown redness of the membrane lining the [[gullet]] and [[trachea|windpipe]], along with symptoms of slight congestion within the [[duodenum]] and stomach. Some toxins are destroyed by drying, and indeed, dried [[hay]] containing the plant is not poisonous at all.<ref name="WebMD" />
